children: By Ross Kerber
The opinions expressed in this column are those of the author, a correspondent for Reuters.
Vanguard is marking the 50th anniversary of the first index fund, now the Vanguard 500 fund
, with hoopla like this webpage. To the firm's credit, it also acknowledges how the idea of passive investing was once derided as "UnAmerican" by critics.
The dig was tongue-in-cheek, I discovered from a few phone calls, but worth reviewing to understand the extent to which these funds broke with what had been conventional wisdom.

Vanguard 500 now boasts some $1.8 trillion in assets. Its origins date from a low point of Jack Bogle's career, after he was fired in 1974 as CEO of Wellington Management for "an unwise merger," as this article puts it.

In the oft-told story, Vanguard founder Bogle staged a comeback by creating funds that tracked a market index, owned by their own investors and able to operate with cheaper fees. Especially during the financial crisis,  the advantages of low fees became apparent to average investors, and Vanguard's scale gave it the power to drive them ever-lower. A Vanguard chart shows the firm's average ETF and mutual fund expense ratio at 0.07% at the end of 2024, versus 0.44% for the industry at the time.

Costs help drive performance. Passive mutual funds outperformed active ones in seven of the last 10 years, according to Morningstar, although active ETFs did better than passive ones in five of those years.

Investors held some $22 trillion in passive funds and ETFs as of July, compared with $17.2 trillion worth of active funds and ETFs, according to Morningstar. That is a huge swing from 1993, the first full year for which Morningstar has data, showing active mutual funds with $1.4 trillion compared with just $27 billion in passive funds.
BOGLE v LEUTHOLD

If Bogle was the visionary, someone quick to grasp his views was a skeptical investment pro in Minneapolis. Steve Leuthold, creator of a research and investment management company bearing his name, was often on the road meeting with portfolio managers and would have been in on talk about the radically different nature of the new passive funds, according to John Mueller, now co-CEO of Leuthold Group.

According to Mueller, the firm sent out end-of-year holiday gifts to clients, and sometime in the early-to-mid-1980s, these included a satirical poster that became a cult hit. It showed Uncle Sam - apparently symbolizing the traditional American investment establishment - frantically stamping the word "UN AMERICAN" onto what looks like reams of continuous-feed computer paper. "Help Stamp Out Index Funds!" reads its headline.

The Uncle Sam figure would have been a familiar sight after the U.S. bicentennial celebrations of 1976, Mueller said. The poster's text likely reflected the appreciation Leuthold was already hearing from investment clients about the new indexed products.

"I’m not sure Steve came up with the concept of funds being un-American, I bet he heard it. He was often on the road talking to money managers and maybe they were griping about index funds," Mueller said. "I don't think they ever thought they would grow to what they became."

Leuthold hired Mueller in 2001; Leuthold died in 2023. The poster, Mueller said, was in line with Leuthold's well-known contrarian streak and sense of humor. “I am contrary but not for the sake of being contrary. It’s good business. When everybody hates something, we buy it. When everybody loves something, we sell it. There is a warm comfort in being part of the herd. But I can live without it," Leuthold said, according to this obituary.

Scott Opsal, Leuthold Group's director of investment strategies, said one legacy of the passive investing movement is how it allows clients to choose their own focus areas, such as through buying thematic ETFs that track particular sectors. "Portfolio control is a huge advantage of the passive wave," he told me.
Despite the poster's sentiments, Opsal said Leuthold actually adopted some of the theories of passive management such as by evaluating stocks as members of different industries.
The phrase "UnAmerican," Opsal said, likely underscored the common criticism that passive funds encouraged people to stop thinking about their money.

"I imagine one of the key motivations behind Steve's thought-provoking poster was that the passive fund movement was promoting the notion of investing without thinking," Opsal said. "The belief that a given asset is a good investment at any price and under any market condition is foolishness, and a theory that sends that message is doing a disservice to the investing public. I suspect Steve’s goal was to reinforce that prices matter and economic conditions matter, and a wise investor should be regularly and actively evaluating their portfolios from that perspective."
BROADER PERSPECTIVE

As long as we're talking index fund impact, an important part of their growth has been their influence on how companies are run. Paul Washington, CEO of the Society for Corporate Governance, which represents corporate secretaries and others in the issuer community, said big index fund leaders carry the most influence among shareholders since they have the broadest perspective and cannot buy and sell stocks based on feelings, analysis or the "animal spirits" cited by economist John Maynard Keynes.

"Conversations with the index funds can be the most valuable inputs you get from investors," Washington said. "They're aware of the practices at other companies and they also have views on systemic risks and opportunities. They're not in and out of your stock, so they have the benefit of continuity."

In a recent survey, about 25% of responding companies said regulatory changes last year made it more challenging for company leaders to speak with institutional investors, he said. The changes pushed by securities regulators nominated by U.S. President Donald Trump have primarily affected index funds.
